analysis.one_liner: Bans former members of Congress from lobbying forever and bars House members from owning individual stocks.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a committee hearing or a vote: it was sent to five House committees on the day it was introduced and died there when the 118th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The HUMBLE Act would have banned former senators, House members, and elected congressional officers from lobbying Congress for the rest of their lives, replacing the current one-to-two-year ban. It would have barred House members from owning individual corporate stocks or sitting on for-profit corporate boards, stripped former House members of perks like the Members' dining room, chamber floor access, and reserved parking, limited official travel to coach-class airfare, and docked members a day of pay for every day a new Congress went without an elected Speaker.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary citizens, whose laws and tax money would no longer be shaped by former lawmakers selling access built on their years in office. It also protects sitting members from the pressure of trading on inside knowledge of pending legislation, since they could no longer hold individual corporate stocks.

how_it_helps.text: It replaces the current one-year (House) or two-year (Senate) lobbying ban with a lifetime ban on former members and elected officers lobbying Congress, removing the revolving door entirely rather than merely delaying it.
It bars House members from owning common stock in individual corporations and from serving on for-profit boards, ending the ability to legislate on matters that directly affect one's own investments.

It strips former House members of privileges not available to the public — House chamber access, athletic facilities, the Members' dining room, and parking — with any waivers from the Speaker and minority leader published in the Congressional Record within 24 hours.

It limits official travel to coach-class airfare and cuts House members' pay by one day's salary for every day a Congress passes without electing a Speaker, responding to the multi-day Speaker stalemates that have repeatedly halted House business.

analysis.who_pays: Current and former members of Congress themselves, and the lobbying firms that hire former lawmakers for their relationships and procedural knowledge. Former members would lose a lucrative post-Congress career path, and sitting members would have to divest individual stock holdings.
analysis.who_pays_short: Members of Congress and lobbying firms

drawbacks.text: A lifetime lobbying ban may go further than needed: the current one-to-two-year cooling-off period already exists, and critics of broad bans argue that former members have expertise that can legitimately inform policy debate, and that a total ban may simply push lobbying activity to former staffers and outside consultants who face weaker restrictions.

The stock ban applies only to the House and only to common stock of individual corporations, leaving diversified funds, Senate members, and other vehicles untouched, so the conflict-of-interest problem would be narrowed rather than eliminated.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits — closing the revolving door between Congress and K Street and removing the ability of lawmakers to trade stocks in companies they regulate — are the kind of reforms that directly address how Congress serves the public. The costs fall almost entirely on members of Congress themselves, which is precisely the group the bill regulates. The main design weaknesses are that the bill was House-only and the stock ban is narrow, but the core provisions are straightforward integrity reforms rather than a badly built policy.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to five House committees the day it was introduced, none of them ever acted on it, and it died when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Angie Craig introduced the HUMBLE Act on January 25, 2023, with one Democratic cosponsor.

The bill was referred to the House Administration, Judiciary, Ethics, Rules, and Oversight and Accountability committees for portions falling under their jurisdiction; a referral to five committees is a heavy procedural burden, since a bill must clear every committee with jurisdiction before it can reach the floor.

No committee reported the bill, no hearing or markup is recorded, and the bill's only recorded action after introduction is the referral itself; it received no vote in the House or Senate before the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Former members of Congress who sell their services as lobbyists, and sitting members who want to keep holding individual stocks and enjoying post-Congress privileges, are better off because the bill never advanced. Lobbying firms that hire former lawmakers retain their current access pipeline.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Former members turned lobbyists and current stock-holding members

for.name: Rep. Angie Craig
for.what_they_did: Introduced the HUMBLE Act proposing a lifetime lobbying ban, a House stock-ownership ban, elimination of former-member perks, coach-only official travel, and Speaker-stalemate pay cuts.

for.name: One Democratic cosponsor
for.what_they_did: Signed on as the bill's only cosponsor.

against.name: House committee chairs (House Administration, Judiciary, Ethics, Rules, Oversight)
against.role: Chairs of the five committees of referral (Republican majority, 118th Congress)
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing, markup, or vote on the bill during the two-year Congress, leaving it to die in committee.

against.name: House Republican leadership
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill to the floor or designated it for consideration under the multi-committee referral.

sides.party_line_note: The record shows only a Democratic sponsor and one Democratic cosponsor, and no votes or floor action, so no partisan breakdown of support or opposition exists — the bill simply never got that far.

industries.note: A lifetime ban on former members lobbying would cut off the most valuable commodity lobbying firms buy: a former lawmaker's relationships and standing with colleagues. The public interest in laws not being steered by ex-lawmakers-for-hire runs directly against that business model.

Former senators, House members, and elected officers would be barred from lobbying for life and would lose chamber, dining room, gym, and parking privileges. Their post-congressional income and privileges depend on the access the bill removes.

Sitting members would lose the ability to hold individual corporate stock, sit on for-profit boards, fly official trips in premium cabins, and keep full pay through Speaker stalemates. These are personal financial interests that conflict with, rather than run alongside, the public's interest in unbiased legislating.
